decks.title: Proteins, Vitamins and Nucleic Acids — Part 1: Amino acids and proteins
goals: Classify amino acids and draw the zwitter ion of an amino acid
Explain the isoelectric point and predict the charge of an amino acid at a given pH
Show the formation of a peptide bond and define the four levels of protein structure
Explain denaturation and state the roles of enzymes and hormones

slides.heading: Molecules of life
slides.body_md: Part 1 — from the twenty amino acids to the proteins they build: hair, muscle, enzymes and hormones.

visual.alt: Table of five proteins, where each works and its job

slides.narration: Namaste! Your hair, your muscles, the enzymes that digest your food and the insulin that controls your blood sugar are all proteins. Every one of them is a chain built from just twenty kinds of amino acid. In this part we meet the amino acids, link them into proteins, and see what happens when a protein loses its shape.

slides.heading: Amino acids and their classification
slides.body_md: Proteins are built from **α-amino acids**, H₂N–CH(R)–COOH: the –NH₂ and –COOH groups are on the same carbon. Except **glycine** (R = H), all are chiral and occur as the **L**-form. **By diet:** **essential** amino acids cannot be made in the body and must come from food (e.g. valine, leucine, lysine, phenylalanine, tryptophan); **non-essential** ones can be made (glycine, alanine, glutamic acid). **By groups:** **neutral** (one –NH₂, one –COOH), **acidic** (extra –COOH), **basic** (extra –NH₂).

visual.alt: Table of neutral, acidic and basic amino acids with examples and side chains

slides.narration: An alpha amino acid has an amino group and a carboxyl group on the same carbon atom, together with a side chain that differs from one amino acid to the next. All except glycine are chiral. Essential amino acids must come from our food because the body cannot make them; non-essential ones can be made in the body. Amino acids are also neutral, acidic or basic, depending on whether they have an extra acid or amino group.

slides.heading: The zwitter ion
slides.body_md: In the solid and in water, the acidic –COOH gives H⁺ to the basic –NH₂ of the same molecule, forming a **dipolar ion (zwitter ion)**, H₃N⁺–CH(R)–COO⁻. This explains the salt-like properties: **high melting points** (with decomposition), **solubility in water** but not in non-polar solvents, and **amphoteric** behaviour — –COO⁻ accepts H⁺ from acids, –NH₃⁺ gives H⁺ to bases.

visual.alt: Flow showing the glycine zwitter ion gaining a proton in acid to form a cation and losing a proton in alkali to form an anion

slides.narration: Inside a single amino acid molecule, the acid group hands a proton to the amino group. The result is a zwitter ion, which carries both a positive and a negative charge but is neutral overall. Because it is really a salt, an amino acid has a high melting point and dissolves in water rather than in benzene. It also reacts with both acids and bases, so it is amphoteric.

slides.heading: Isoelectric point
slides.body_md: The **isoelectric point (pI)** is the pH at which an amino acid exists mainly as the zwitter ion, has **no net charge** and does **not move** in an electric field. Below its pI an amino acid is mainly a **cation** (moves to the cathode); above its pI it is mainly an **anion** (moves to the anode). For a neutral amino acid, pI is the average of the two pKa values.

visual.alt: Table of four amino acids with their type and approximate isoelectric point

slides.narration: Every amino acid has a particular pH, its isoelectric point, at which it is almost entirely the zwitter ion and does not move when a voltage is applied. In more acidic solutions it picks up a proton and becomes positive, so it moves towards the cathode. In more alkaline solutions it loses a proton and becomes negative. Acidic amino acids have low isoelectric points and basic ones high.

slides.heading: Worked example: which way does it move?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A mixture of glutamic acid (pI 3.2), glycine (pI 6.0) and lysine (pI 9.7) is placed in a buffer of pH 6.0 between two electrodes. Predict the movement of each.

**Glutamic acid:** pH 6.0 > pI → net negative → moves to the **anode**.

**Glycine:** pH = pI → no net charge → **stays** in place.

**Lysine:** pH 6.0 < pI → net positive → moves to the **cathode**.

This is the basis of **electrophoresis**, used to separate amino acids and proteins.

visual.alt: Table predicting the charge and direction of movement of three amino acids at pH 6

slides.narration: Compare the pH of the buffer with each isoelectric point. Glutamic acid sits in a solution more alkaline than its isoelectric point, so it is negative and moves to the anode. Glycine is at its isoelectric point and stays put. Lysine is in a solution more acidic than its isoelectric point, so it is positive and moves to the cathode. This separation is called electrophoresis.

slides.heading: Quick check: amino acids
slides.body_md: Identify the form of an amino acid at a given pH.
slides.narration: Quick check. At the isoelectric point both groups are ionised and the net charge is zero.

slides.heading: The peptide bond
slides.body_md: The –COOH of one amino acid condenses with the –NH₂ of the next, losing H₂O, to form an amide link, **–CO–NH–**, called a **peptide bond**. Two amino acids give a **dipeptide**, three a tripeptide; many give a **polypeptide**. A chain of n amino acids has **n − 1** peptide bonds. The chain has a free –NH₂ (**N-terminal**, written on the left) and a free –COOH (**C-terminal**, on the right).

slides.narration: When the acid group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of another, a molecule of water is lost and an amide link forms between them. In proteins this link is called a peptide bond. Two amino acids make a dipeptide, and many make a polypeptide. A chain of n amino acids has one fewer peptide bond than it has amino acids. By convention the end with the free amino group is written on the left.

slides.heading: Worked example: a tripeptide
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Glycine ($M = 75$), alanine ($M = 89$) and valine ($M = 117$) join to form the tripeptide Gly–Ala–Val. (a) How many peptide bonds and water molecules are involved? (b) What is the molar mass of the tripeptide? (c) How many different tripeptides can be made using each of the three amino acids once?

**(a)** 3 − 1 = **2** peptide bonds and **2** molecules of $\ce{H2O}$ released.

**(b)** $M = 75 + 89 + 117 - 2 \times 18 = 245\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.

**(c)** $3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$ sequences (Gly–Ala–Val, Gly–Val–Ala, Ala–Gly–Val, …).

visual.alt: Table of answers for the tripeptide example

slides.narration: Three amino acids are joined by two peptide bonds, and each bond releases one water molecule. So the molar mass of the tripeptide is the sum of the three amino acids minus two waters, which gives two hundred and forty five. Since the order matters, three different amino acids can be arranged in six different sequences, each a different tripeptide.

slides.heading: Quick check: peptide bonds
slides.body_md: Locate the peptide bond in a dipeptide.
slides.narration: Quick check. The peptide bond joins the acid group of one unit to the amino group of the next.

slides.heading: Proteins: classes and levels of structure
slides.body_md: **Fibrous** proteins: long parallel chains held by hydrogen and disulfide bonds; insoluble; structural (keratin, collagen, myosin). **Globular** proteins: chains folded into compact, roughly spherical shapes; water-soluble; functional (insulin, albumin, enzymes). **Levels of structure (definitions):** **primary** — the sequence of amino acids; **secondary** — regular folding of the chain into an α-helix or β-pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds; **tertiary** — the overall three-dimensional folding of one chain; **quaternary** — the arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits (haemoglobin has four).

rows: The 51 residues of insulin in order

visual.alt: Table defining the four levels of protein structure with an example of each

slides.narration: Fibrous proteins such as keratin have long chains lying side by side and are insoluble, so they build structures. Globular proteins such as insulin are folded into compact shapes and dissolve in water, so they can work in body fluids. Protein structure is described at four levels: the sequence of amino acids, the regular helix or sheet, the overall folding of each chain, and the arrangement of several chains together.

slides.heading: Denaturation
slides.body_md: When a globular protein is exposed to **heat**, a **change of pH**, **alcohol** or **heavy-metal ions**, its hydrogen bonds and other interactions break, so the **secondary and tertiary** (and quaternary) structure is lost. The **primary structure (peptide bonds) remains**. The protein becomes insoluble and **loses its biological activity**. Examples: coagulation of egg white on boiling; curdling of milk as lactic acid forms; 70% alcohol killing bacteria.

nodes.label: Heat, acid or alkali, alcohol, Hg²⁺/Pb²⁺

visual.alt: Flow of denaturation from a folded active protein to an unfolded inactive one

slides.narration: A protein works only when it is folded into the right shape. Heat, strong acids or alkalis, alcohol and heavy metal ions break the hydrogen bonds and other forces that hold this shape. The chain unfolds and the protein loses its activity, although the sequence of amino acids is not changed. Boiled egg white, sour milk and alcohol disinfectants are all examples of denaturation.

slides.heading: Enzymes and hormones
slides.body_md: **Enzymes** are biological catalysts, almost all **globular proteins**. They are **highly specific**, very efficient, and work best at about body temperature and an **optimum pH**; they lower the activation energy. Examples: invertase (sucrose → glucose + fructose), maltase, pepsin (proteins → peptides), urease (urea → NH₃ + CO₂). **Hormones** are chemical messengers made by endocrine glands and carried in the blood: **insulin** (lowers blood glucose), **glucagon** (raises it), **thyroxine** (controls metabolic rate; contains iodine), **adrenaline** (emergency response), and steroid sex hormones.

visual.alt: Table of two enzymes and three hormones with their roles

slides.narration: Enzymes are the catalysts of living cells, and nearly all are globular proteins. Each acts on one particular substance or reaction, and each works best at a certain temperature and pH. Urease, for example, breaks down urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide. Hormones are chemical messengers released by glands into the blood. Insulin lowers blood sugar, glucagon raises it, and thyroxine controls the rate of metabolism.

slides.heading: Quick check: denaturation and enzymes
slides.body_md: Decide what denaturation changes and what it leaves intact.
slides.narration: Quick check. Denaturation unfolds the chain but does not break peptide bonds.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: α-Amino acids H₂N–CH(R)–COOH: essential or non-essential; neutral, acidic or basic; all chiral except glycine.
Zwitter ion H₃N⁺–CH(R)–COO⁻: high m.p., water-soluble, amphoteric; no net charge at the isoelectric point.
Peptide bond –CO–NH–; n amino acids → n − 1 bonds; fibrous vs globular proteins.
Denaturation destroys 2°/3° structure, not 1°; enzymes are specific protein catalysts; hormones are chemical messengers.

visual.alt: Summary table of four key ideas from Part 1

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Amino acids exist as zwitter ions, which explains their salt-like and amphoteric properties, and each has an isoelectric point. Peptide bonds join them into polypeptides and proteins, whose structure is described at four levels. Denaturation unfolds a protein without breaking its peptide bonds. Enzymes are protein catalysts, and hormones are chemical messengers.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Draw the zwitter ion with both charges shown: H₃N⁺ and COO⁻.
Below pI → cation → cathode; above pI → anion → anode.
For a peptide, mark the –CO–NH– bond and write the N-terminal residue first.
Denaturation never changes the amino acid sequence.

rows: n amino acids, n peptide bonds

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and fixes

slides.narration: Some tips. When you draw a zwitter ion, show both charges. Link pH to charge carefully: below the isoelectric point the amino acid is positive. A chain of n amino acids has one fewer peptide bond than amino acids. And remember that denaturation changes the shape of a protein, never its sequence.

decks.title: Proteins, Vitamins and Nucleic Acids — Part 2: Vitamins and nucleic acids
goals: Classify vitamins A, B, C, D, E and K as fat-soluble or water-soluble
Match each vitamin with its main function and deficiency disease
Name the purine and pyrimidine bases and describe the DNA double helix
Compare DNA and RNA in sugar, bases, structure and function

slides.heading: Small needs, big effects
slides.body_md: Part 2 — vitamins, needed in tiny amounts, and the nucleic acids that carry the instructions for every protein.

visual.alt: Flow from DNA to RNA to proteins, many of which need vitamins to function

slides.narration: In Part 2 we look at vitamins, which the body needs only in small amounts but cannot do without, and at the nucleic acids. DNA stores the instructions for making every protein, and RNA carries those instructions out. Many of the enzymes made this way need vitamins to work.

slides.heading: Vitamins: fat-soluble and water-soluble
slides.body_md: **Vitamins** are organic compounds needed in **small amounts** in the diet for normal growth and health; most cannot be made in the body. **Fat-soluble: A, D, E, K** — stored in the liver and fatty tissue, so large excesses can be harmful. **Water-soluble: B group and C** — not stored (excess is excreted in urine), so they must be supplied **regularly**; they are also easily lost when vegetables are boiled and the water discarded. (Vitamin B₁₂ is an exception: it is stored in the liver.)

visual.alt: Table comparing fat-soluble and water-soluble vitamins by members, storage and supply

slides.narration: Vitamins are organic substances we need in tiny amounts. They fall into two groups. Vitamins A, D, E and K dissolve in fat and are stored in the liver and fatty tissue, so we do not need them every day, and too much can build up and cause harm. The B vitamins and vitamin C dissolve in water and are passed out in urine, so they must be eaten regularly.

slides.heading: Functions and deficiency diseases
slides.body_md: Each vitamin has characteristic sources and a characteristic deficiency disease.

rows: Citrus fruits, amla, green leafy vegetables
Sunlight on skin, fish, egg yolk
Rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults
Fragile red blood cells, muscular weakness

visual.alt: Table of vitamins A, B1, B2, B6, B12, C, D, E and K with sources and deficiency diseases

slides.narration: This table links each vitamin to its sources and to the disease caused when it is missing. Lack of vitamin A causes night blindness. Shortage of the B vitamins causes beriberi, cracked lips, convulsions or pernicious anaemia. Lack of vitamin C causes scurvy, of vitamin D rickets, of vitamin E fragile red blood cells, and of vitamin K slow clotting of blood.

slides.heading: Quick check: deficiency diseases
slides.body_md: Link a deficiency symptom with the vitamin.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about which vitamin is needed for blood to clot.

slides.heading: Worked example: diagnosing a deficiency
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Name the vitamin most likely to be lacking: (a) a sailor on a long voyage with only dried food develops swollen, bleeding gums; (b) a child kept indoors in a smoggy city has soft, bowed leg bones; (c) a patient whose wound keeps bleeding for a long time; (d) a strict vegan for many years becomes anaemic.

**(a)** Vitamin C — scurvy. **(b)** Vitamin D — rickets. **(c)** Vitamin K — slow clotting. **(d)** Vitamin B₁₂ — pernicious anaemia (found mainly in animal foods).

visual.alt: Table matching four cases to the vitamin lacking and the condition

slides.narration: Work from the symptom to the vitamin. Bleeding gums on a long voyage without fresh food point to scurvy and a lack of vitamin C. Soft, bent bones in a child who gets little sunlight point to rickets and vitamin D. Slow clotting points to vitamin K. And because vitamin B twelve comes mainly from animal foods, a strict vegan diet can lead to pernicious anaemia.

slides.heading: Quick check: vitamin groups
slides.body_md: Sort vitamins into fat-soluble and water-soluble groups.
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember the four fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E and K.

slides.heading: Nucleic acids: nucleotides and bases
slides.body_md: **Nucleic acids** (DNA and RNA) are polymers of **nucleotides**. Each nucleotide = **nitrogenous base + pentose sugar + phosphate**; base + sugar alone is a **nucleoside**. Nucleotides are joined through phosphate groups (phosphodiester links) into a sugar–phosphate backbone. **Sugar:** 2-deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA. **Bases:** **purines** (two rings) — **adenine (A)** and **guanine (G)**, in both; **pyrimidines** (one ring) — **cytosine (C)** in both, **thymine (T)** in DNA only, **uracil (U)** in RNA only.

visual.alt: Table of the five nucleic-acid bases, purine or pyrimidine, and whether each occurs in DNA and RNA

slides.narration: Nucleic acids are long chains of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has three parts: a nitrogen-containing base, a five-carbon sugar and a phosphate group. The sugar is deoxyribose in DNA and ribose in RNA. Adenine and guanine are the larger purine bases, found in both. Cytosine is a pyrimidine found in both, but thymine occurs only in DNA, and uracil takes its place in RNA.

slides.heading: The DNA double helix
slides.body_md: Watson and Crick (1953): DNA is a **double helix** of two polynucleotide strands wound round a common axis, with the sugar–phosphate backbones outside and the bases inside. The strands are **antiparallel** and **complementary**: **A pairs with T** (two hydrogen bonds) and **G pairs with C** (three hydrogen bonds), always a purine with a pyrimidine. Hence in any double-stranded DNA, A = T and G = C (**Chargaff’s rule**).

slides.narration: In nineteen fifty three Watson and Crick showed that DNA is a double helix, like a twisted ladder. The two sugar phosphate backbones form the sides and run in opposite directions. The rungs are pairs of bases held by hydrogen bonds: adenine always pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds, and guanine with cytosine through three. So the two strands are complementary, and the amounts of adenine and thymine are always equal.

slides.heading: Worked example: base counting
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A double-stranded DNA molecule has 2000 base pairs and contains 560 adenine bases. How many (a) thymine, (b) cytosine and (c) guanine bases does it contain?

**(a)** T = A = **560**.

**(b)** Total bases $= 2 \times 2000 = 4000$; G + C $= 4000 - 2 \times 560 = 2880$; C $= 2880 \div 2 = 1440$.

**(c)** G = C = **1440**.

visual.alt: Table of the numbers of each base in a DNA molecule of 2000 base pairs

slides.narration: Each base pair contains two bases, so two thousand pairs means four thousand bases. Thymine equals adenine, five hundred and sixty. Taking adenine and thymine away leaves two thousand eight hundred and eighty bases shared equally between guanine and cytosine, so each is one thousand four hundred and forty.

slides.heading: Quick check: bases
slides.body_md: Classify bases as purines or pyrimidines.
slides.narration: Quick check. The purines are adenine and guanine.

slides.heading: RNA, and DNA compared with RNA
slides.body_md: **RNA** is usually a **single strand**. Three main types work in protein synthesis: **messenger RNA (mRNA)** carries the coded message from DNA; **transfer RNA (tRNA)** brings amino acids to the ribosome; **ribosomal RNA (rRNA)** forms part of the ribosome. **DNA** stores hereditary information and **replicates** itself, so the information passes to daughter cells.

visual.alt: Table comparing DNA and RNA by sugar, bases, strands, function and location

slides.narration: RNA is usually a single strand. Messenger RNA carries the coded instructions from DNA, transfer RNA brings the matching amino acids, and ribosomal RNA forms part of the ribosome where proteins are assembled. DNA is the long-term store of genetic information and can copy itself, so that each new cell receives the same instructions.

slides.heading: Worked example: an RNA copy
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** An RNA strand is copied from a DNA strand whose base sequence is T–A–C–C–G–A. (a) Write the RNA sequence. (b) Which base of the RNA has no partner base of the same name in DNA?

**(a)** Pair each DNA base: T → A, A → **U**, C → G, G → C. RNA: **A–U–G–G–C–U**.

**(b)** **Uracil**: RNA uses U where DNA uses T.

visual.alt: Table of DNA bases and the RNA bases that pair with them

slides.narration: RNA is built using the DNA strand as a template, following the pairing rules, except that RNA uses uracil wherever thymine would appear. So each adenine in DNA is matched by uracil in RNA, each thymine by adenine, each cytosine by guanine and each guanine by cytosine. The sequence T A C C G A gives the RNA A U G G C U.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K are stored; water-soluble B and C must be supplied regularly.
A: night blindness; B₁: beriberi; B₁₂: pernicious anaemia; C: scurvy; D: rickets; K: slow clotting.
Nucleotide = base + sugar + phosphate; purines A, G; pyrimidines C, T (DNA), U (RNA).
DNA: double helix, antiparallel complementary strands; A–T (2 H-bonds), G–C (3).
RNA: single strand, ribose, uracil; mRNA, tRNA, rRNA in protein synthesis.

visual.alt: Summary table of base pairs and hydrogen bonds

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble and stored; the B vitamins and vitamin C are water-soluble and needed regularly. Each vitamin has its own deficiency disease. Nucleic acids are chains of nucleotides; DNA is a double helix held by base pairing, and RNA, with ribose and uracil, carries out protein synthesis.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Learn the vitamin–disease pairs as a table; most objective questions test them.
Explain storage differences using solubility in fat or water.
In base calculations, double the base-pair count to get total bases.
Compare DNA and RNA on sugar, bases, strands and function — one mark each.

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 2 and fixes

slides.narration: Final tips. Learn the vitamins and their deficiency diseases as a table. Explain storage in terms of whether the vitamin dissolves in fat or water. In base-counting problems, remember that each base pair contains two bases. And when comparing DNA with RNA, give the sugar, the bases, the number of strands and the function.

notes.title: Proteins, Vitamins and Nucleic Acids — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Amino acids
sections.body_md:
**α-Amino acids** H₂N–CH(R)–COOH; all chiral (L) except glycine. **Essential** (from diet: valine, leucine, isoleucine, lysine, threonine, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, arginine, histidine) vs **non-essential** (made in the body: glycine, alanine, glutamic acid). **Neutral** (one –NH₂, one –COOH), **acidic** (extra –COOH: aspartic, glutamic acid), **basic** (extra –NH₂: lysine, arginine).

**Zwitter ion** H₃N⁺–CH(R)–COO⁻: salt-like — high m.p., soluble in water not benzene, **amphoteric**. **Isoelectric point (pI):** pH of zero net charge, no migration in an electric field; below pI → cation (to cathode), above pI → anion (to anode). For neutral amino acids pI ≈ (pKa₁ + pKa₂)/2.

key_terms.definition_md: A dipolar ion carrying both a positive (–NH₃⁺) and a negative (–COO⁻) charge, neutral overall.
The pH at which an amino acid has no net charge and does not move in an electric field.

visual.alt: Table of amino-acid form and migration at pH below, at and above the isoelectric point

sections.heading: 2. Peptides and proteins
sections.body_md:
**Peptide bond** –CO–NH– from –COOH of one amino acid + –NH₂ of the next, losing H₂O. n amino acids → **n − 1** peptide bonds and n − 1 H₂O; M(peptide) = ΣM(amino acids) − 18(n − 1). N-terminal (free –NH₂) written on the left.

**Fibrous** (keratin, collagen, myosin): parallel chains, H- and disulfide bonds, insoluble, structural. **Globular** (insulin, albumin, enzymes): compact folded chains, soluble, functional.

**Levels (definitions only):** primary — amino-acid sequence; secondary — α-helix or β-pleated sheet (H-bonds); tertiary — overall 3D folding of a chain; quaternary — arrangement of subunits (haemoglobin: four).

key_terms.definition_md: The amide link –CO–NH– joining two amino-acid residues.
The sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain.

visual.alt: Table comparing fibrous and globular proteins

sections.heading: 3. Denaturation, enzymes and hormones
sections.body_md:
**Denaturation:** heat, pH change, alcohol or heavy-metal ions break H-bonds and other interactions; 2°, 3° (and 4°) structure lost, **1° intact**; protein coagulates and loses activity (boiled egg, curdled milk, 70% alcohol on bacteria).

**Enzymes:** biological catalysts, mostly globular proteins; highly specific, efficient, work best near body temperature and an optimum pH; lower activation energy. Invertase (sucrose), maltase (maltose), pepsin (proteins → peptides), urease: $\ce{NH2CONH2 + H2O -> 2NH3 + CO2}$.

**Hormones:** chemical messengers from endocrine glands carried in blood — insulin (lowers blood glucose), glucagon (raises it), thyroxine (metabolic rate; contains iodine), adrenaline (emergency), steroid sex hormones.

key_terms.definition_md: Loss of the secondary and tertiary structure, and of biological activity, of a protein without breaking peptide bonds.
A biological catalyst, usually a globular protein, specific for its substrate.

visual.alt: Table of three hormones and their roles

sections.heading: 4. Vitamins
sections.body_md:
**Fat-soluble:** A, D, E, K (stored in liver and fat; excess can be harmful). **Water-soluble:** B group, C (excreted; must be supplied regularly; lost in cooking water). B₁₂ is stored in the liver.

| Vitamin | Deficiency |
|---|---|
| A | Night blindness, xerophthalmia |
| B₁ | Beriberi |
| B₂ | Cheilosis, digestive disorders |
| B₆ | Convulsions |
| B₁₂ | Pernicious anaemia |
| C | Scurvy (bleeding gums) |
| D | Rickets (children), osteomalacia (adults) |
| E | Fragile red blood cells, muscular weakness |
| K | Increased blood-clotting time |

key_terms.definition_md: An organic compound needed in small amounts in the diet for normal growth and health.
One of vitamins A, D, E and K, which dissolve in fat and are stored in the body.

visual.alt: Table of vitamin groups

sections.heading: 5. Nucleic acids
sections.body_md:
**Nucleotide** = base + pentose + phosphate (nucleoside = base + sugar); joined by phosphodiester links. **Purines:** adenine, guanine. **Pyrimidines:** cytosine, thymine (DNA), uracil (RNA).

**DNA:** 2-deoxyribose; double helix (Watson and Crick, 1953); antiparallel, complementary strands; A–T (2 H-bonds), G–C (3 H-bonds); A = T, G = C. Stores hereditary information; replicates.

**RNA:** ribose; A, G, C, U; usually single-stranded; mRNA (message), tRNA (carries amino acids), rRNA (ribosome); protein synthesis.

Base counting: total bases = 2 × base pairs.

key_terms.definition_md: The monomer of nucleic acids: a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group.
Two DNA strands whose bases pair A with T and G with C.

visual.alt: Table comparing DNA and RNA

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving the zwitter ion a net charge, or confusing which way an amino acid moves below its pI.
- Counting n peptide bonds for n amino acids (it is n − 1).
- Saying denaturation breaks peptide bonds.
- Listing vitamin C as fat-soluble, or putting thymine in RNA.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Zwitter ion (1 mark): correct charges; amphoteric equations (1 mark each).
- Vitamins (½–1 mark each): vitamin, group and deficiency disease.
- DNA vs RNA (1 mark per feature): sugar, bases, strands, function.

cards.back_md: One the body cannot make; must come from food.

Highly specific; work best at optimum temperature and pH.
Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it.

questions.stem_md: In an aqueous solution kept at its isoelectric point, glycine exists mainly as:
questions.solution_md: At the pI both groups are ionised and the net charge is zero — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of these amino acids is essential, so that it must be obtained from food such as pulses, milk or eggs?
questions.solution_md: Lysine cannot be made in the human body — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Aspartic acid, HOOC–CH₂–CH(NH₂)–COOH, is classified as:
questions.solution_md: Two –COOH groups and one –NH₂ group — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Lysine has an isoelectric point of 9.7. In a buffer of pH 6.0 placed between two electrodes, lysine:

options.text_md: carries a net positive charge and moves towards the cathode
carries a net negative charge and moves towards the anode
has no net charge and does not move
carries a net positive charge and moves towards the anode

questions.solution_md: pH below pI → cation → cathode — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which α-amino acid found in proteins is optically inactive?
questions.solution_md: The α-carbon of glycine carries two H atoms, so it is not chiral — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Alanine reacts both with dilute hydrochloric acid and with dilute sodium hydroxide solution.
questions.solution_md: True: the zwitter ion is amphoteric.

questions.stem_md: The pH at which an amino acid such as alanine carries no net charge and does not move in an electric field is called its ___ point.
questions.solution_md: **Isoelectric** point.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Glycine dissolves in water but is almost insoluble in benzene.

**Reason (R):** In the solid state and in water, glycine exists as a dipolar ion.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the ionic (salt-like) nature explains the solubility — option (a).

questions.stem_md: For alanine, $\text{p}K_{a1} = 2.34$ (–COOH) and $\text{p}K_{a2} = 9.69$ (–NH₃⁺). Taking the isoelectric point of a neutral amino acid as the mean of these two values, calculate the pI of alanine.

marking_scheme.step: Mean of the two pKa values

questions.stem_md: Write the zwitter ion of alanine, and give equations to show how it reacts with (a) H⁺ ions and (b) OH⁻ ions.

answer.model_answer_md: Zwitter ion: $\ce{CH3CH(NH3+)COO-}$. (a) $\ce{CH3CH(NH3+)COO- + H+ -> CH3CH(NH3+)COOH}$ (–COO⁻ acts as a base). (b) $\ce{CH3CH(NH3+)COO- + OH- -> CH3CH(NH2)COO- + H2O}$ (–NH₃⁺ acts as an acid).

questions.solution_md: Zwitter ion; two equations.

questions.stem_md: Classify amino acids (a) on the basis of whether the body can make them and (b) on the basis of the numbers of –NH₂ and –COOH groups, giving one example of each class. (c) Why is glycine the only common amino acid that is not optically active?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Essential (must be in the diet), e.g. valine or lysine; non-essential (made in the body), e.g. glycine or alanine. (b) Neutral (equal numbers), e.g. alanine; acidic (more –COOH), e.g. glutamic acid; basic (more –NH₂), e.g. lysine. (c) In glycine R = H, so the α-carbon carries two identical H atoms and is not chiral.

questions.solution_md: Two classifications with examples; glycine not chiral.

questions.stem_md: (a) Explain why amino acids are amphoteric. (b) What is meant by the isoelectric point? (c) Glutamic acid has a pI of 3.2. Towards which electrode will it move at pH 7, and why?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) They exist as zwitter ions H₃N⁺–CH(R)–COO⁻: the –COO⁻ group accepts a proton from acids and the –NH₃⁺ group donates a proton to bases. (b) The pH at which the amino acid exists mainly as the zwitter ion with no net charge, so it does not migrate in an electric field. (c) pH 7 is above its pI, so it loses a proton and carries a net negative charge: it moves to the anode.

questions.solution_md: Zwitter ion; definition; anode.

questions.stem_md: In the dipeptide glycylalanine, H₂NCH₂CO–NHCH(CH₃)COOH, the peptide bond is formed between:

options.text_md: the –NH₂ group of glycine and the –COOH group of alanine
the –COOH groups of both amino acids
the α-carbon atoms of the two amino acids
the –COOH group of glycine and the –NH₂ group of alanine

questions.solution_md: Glycine is written first (N-terminal), so its carboxyl group forms the amide link — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The exact order in which the 51 amino-acid residues are joined in the two chains of insulin is called the protein’s:
questions.solution_md: Sequence = primary structure — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Haemoglobin is made of four polypeptide subunits held together in a definite spatial arrangement. This arrangement is its:
questions.solution_md: Arrangement of subunits — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Serum albumin dissolves in water, whereas the keratin of wool does not. The best explanation is that:

options.text_md: keratin is a carbohydrate, not a protein
albumin has a quaternary structure and keratin has none
albumin is globular, its chains folded into a compact shape, while keratin is fibrous, with long parallel chains held together by hydrogen and disulfide bonds

questions.solution_md: Shape and inter-chain bonding decide solubility — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The α-helix and the β-pleated sheet are forms of the tertiary structure of proteins.
questions.solution_md: False: they are forms of the secondary structure.

questions.stem_md: When a tripeptide is written as Gly–Ala–Val, glycine carries the free –NH₂ group and is called the ___-terminal residue.
questions.solution_md: **N**-terminal.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A tetrapeptide contains three peptide bonds.

**Reason (R):** Each peptide bond is formed with the loss of one molecule of water.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but A follows from four units being joined by three links, not from the loss of water — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Match each level of protein structure with its description.

match_right.text_md: α-Helix or β-pleated sheet held by hydrogen bonds
Overall three-dimensional folding of one chain

questions.solution_md: Primary → sequence; secondary → helix or sheet; tertiary → overall folding; quaternary → subunits.

questions.stem_md: Glycine ($M = 75$), alanine ($M = 89$) and serine ($M = 105$) join to form the tripeptide Gly–Ala–Ser. Calculate its molar mass in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$. ($\ce{H2O}$: $M = 18$)
questions.solution_md: Two peptide bonds release two $\ce{H2O}$: $M = 75 + 89 + 105 - 2 \times 18 = 233$.

questions.stem_md: How many different tripeptides can be formed from valine, leucine and serine if each amino acid is used exactly once in every tripeptide?
questions.solution_md: Number of sequences $= 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$.

questions.stem_md: Human insulin has two polypeptide chains, one of 21 and one of 30 amino-acid residues. How many peptide bonds does it contain in total?
Write an equation for the formation of the dipeptide alanylglycine from alanine and glycine, and identify the peptide bond.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{CH3CH(NH2)COOH + H2NCH2COOH -> CH3CH(NH2)CONHCH2COOH + H2O}$. The –CO–NH– group joining the alanine carbonyl to the glycine nitrogen is the peptide bond.

questions.solution_md: Equation with water; –CO–NH–.

questions.stem_md: Define (a) the secondary structure and (b) the quaternary structure of a protein, naming one protein or feature as an example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Secondary: regular folding of the polypeptide chain into an α-helix or β-pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds between –CO– and –NH– groups — e.g. the α-helix in keratin. (b) Quaternary: the spatial arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits — e.g. the four subunits of haemoglobin.

questions.solution_md: Two definitions with examples.

questions.stem_md: For the tripeptide Gly–Ala–Val (glycine $M = 75$, alanine $M = 89$, valine $M = 117$): (a) state the number of peptide bonds, (b) calculate its molar mass and (c) name the N-terminal and C-terminal residues.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Two. (b) $M = 75 + 89 + 117 - 2 \times 18 = 245\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. (c) N-terminal: glycine; C-terminal: valine.

questions.solution_md: 2; 245; Gly and Val.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Show, with an equation, the formation of the dipeptide glycylalanine, and name the bond formed. [2]

(b) Define the primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures of proteins. [2]

(c) Classify keratin and insulin as fibrous or globular proteins. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\ce{H2NCH2COOH + H2NCH(CH3)COOH -> H2NCH2CONHCH(CH3)COOH + H2O}$; the –CO–NH– link is a peptide (amide) bond.

(b) Primary: sequence of amino acids. Secondary: α-helix or β-pleated sheet held by hydrogen bonds. Tertiary: overall three-dimensional folding of one chain. Quaternary: arrangement of two or more subunits.

(c) Keratin: fibrous. Insulin: globular.

questions.solution_md: Equation; four definitions; classification.

questions.stem_md: A 70% ethanol hand rub kills bacteria by denaturing their proteins. During this denaturation, which bonds remain intact?

options.text_md: The hydrogen bonds holding the α-helices
The peptide bonds of the polypeptide chains
The interactions that maintain the tertiary folding

questions.solution_md: Denaturation leaves the primary structure intact — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A person who has swallowed a solution of a mercury(II) salt is quickly given milk or raw egg white to drink. This first-aid measure works because:

options.text_md: milk proteins reduce Hg²⁺ ions to harmless mercury vapour
egg white contains enzymes that hydrolyse mercury salts
the proteins neutralise the acid formed by mercury salts
the Hg²⁺ ions denature and precipitate the milk or egg proteins instead of the body’s own proteins

questions.solution_md: Heavy-metal ions bind to and precipitate proteins — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Urease catalyses the hydrolysis of urea to ammonia and carbon dioxide but has no effect on its close relative methylurea. This shows that enzymes are:

options.text_md: used up in the reactions they catalyse

questions.solution_md: Each enzyme acts on a particular substrate — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Pepsin, which works in the acidic conditions of the stomach, catalyses the:

options.text_md: hydrolysis of sucrose into glucose and fructose
hydrolysis of proteins into smaller peptides
oxidation of glucose to carbon dioxide

questions.solution_md: Pepsin is a protease — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Several hours after a meal, blood glucose begins to fall and the pancreas releases glucagon. Glucagon acts by:

options.text_md: converting blood glucose into glycogen, lowering blood glucose
promoting the breakdown of liver glycogen, raising blood glucose
increasing the absorption of iodine by the thyroid
catalysing the hydrolysis of sucrose in the gut

questions.solution_md: Glucagon opposes insulin — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A student suddenly sees a snake on the path; her heart races and her blood glucose rises within seconds. The hormone mainly responsible is:
questions.solution_md: Adrenaline prepares the body for emergency — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? An enzyme molecule is used up in the reaction it catalyses and must be replaced after each reaction.
questions.solution_md: False: like any catalyst, the enzyme is regenerated and used again.

questions.stem_md: The enzyme ___ converts urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide.
questions.solution_md: **Urease**.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A denatured enzyme loses its catalytic activity.

**Reason (R):** Denaturation destroys the secondary and tertiary structure on which the shape of the active site depends.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Using the idea of denaturation, explain why (a) 70% alcohol is used to disinfect skin before an injection and (b) an enzyme from the human body stops working when heated above about 60 °C.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Alcohol breaks hydrogen bonds and other interactions in bacterial proteins, unfolding them so the bacteria die. (b) Heat denatures the enzyme: its secondary and tertiary structure (and so the active site) is lost, although the peptide bonds remain.

questions.solution_md: Alcohol and heat both unfold proteins.

questions.stem_md: Write the equation for the hydrolysis of urea catalysed by urease, and state two ways in which enzymes differ from inorganic catalysts such as finely divided nickel.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{NH2CONH2 + H2O ->[urease] 2NH3 + CO2}$. Enzymes are highly specific (one substrate or reaction); they work under mild conditions (body temperature, near-neutral or optimum pH) and are destroyed by heat; they are far more efficient. (Any two.)

questions.solution_md: Equation; two differences.

questions.stem_md: What are hormones? Name the two pancreatic hormones that control blood glucose, and state the effect of each.

answer.model_answer_md: Hormones are chemical messengers produced by endocrine glands and carried in the blood to act on target organs. Insulin lowers blood glucose (promotes uptake and storage as glycogen); glucagon raises it (promotes glycogen breakdown in the liver).

questions.solution_md: Definition; insulin and glucagon.

questions.stem_md: A biology class tests the enzyme amylase from saliva on starch at 37 °C, at 80 °C, and at 37 °C in strongly acidic solution. (a) In which experiment is starch digested fastest? (b) Explain the result at 80 °C. (c) Explain the result in strongly acidic solution.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) At 37 °C (near body temperature and the optimum pH of saliva). (b) At 80 °C the amylase is denatured: hydrogen bonds break, the folded shape and active site are lost, so it no longer catalyses the hydrolysis. (c) The strongly acidic pH is far from the optimum; it changes the charges on the protein and denatures or inactivates it, so little starch is digested.

questions.solution_md: 37 °C fastest; heat and acid denature the enzyme.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by denaturation of a protein? Name two agents that cause it. [2]

(b) Which level of protein structure is unaffected by denaturation, and why? [1]

(c) What are enzymes? State two characteristics and name one enzyme with its reaction. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Loss of the secondary and tertiary (and quaternary) structure of a protein, with loss of biological activity, when hydrogen bonds and other interactions are broken. Agents: heat, change of pH (acid or alkali), alcohol, heavy-metal ions (any two).

(b) The primary structure: denaturation does not break the covalent peptide bonds, so the amino-acid sequence is unchanged.

(c) Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly globular proteins. They are highly specific and work best at an optimum temperature and pH. Urease: $\ce{NH2CONH2 + H2O -> 2NH3 + CO2}$.

questions.solution_md: Definition and agents; primary structure; enzymes.

questions.stem_md: Which set consists only of fat-soluble vitamins?
questions.solution_md: A, D, E, K are fat-soluble; B group and C are water-soluble — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A child whose diet lacks milk, carrots and green vegetables finds it hard to see in dim light, and her eyes become dry. The vitamin most likely lacking is:
questions.solution_md: Night blindness and xerophthalmia — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Before an operation, a patient whose cuts take unusually long to stop bleeding is given a vitamin injection. The vitamin is most likely:
questions.solution_md: Vitamin K is needed for blood clotting — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Several children in a town with heavy winter smog, who rarely play outdoors, develop soft, bow-shaped leg bones. The deficiency is most likely of:
questions.solution_md: Vitamin D is made in skin exposed to sunlight; lack causes rickets — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Pernicious anaemia, in which red blood cells are deficient in haemoglobin, results from a lack of:
questions.solution_md: Option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Deficiency of vitamin E increases the fragility of red blood cells and can cause muscular weakness.
questions.solution_md: True.

questions.stem_md: Sailors on long voyages without fresh fruit once suffered from ___, marked by swollen, bleeding gums, caused by lack of vitamin C.
questions.solution_md: **Scurvy**.

questions.stem_md: Match each deficiency symptom with the vitamin whose lack causes it.
questions.solution_md: Cheilosis → B₂; convulsions → B₆; fragile RBCs → E; slow clotting → K.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Vitamin D need not be eaten every day in a normal diet.

**Reason (R):** Vitamin D is water-soluble.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true (it is stored, and made in skin in sunlight); R is false: vitamin D is fat-soluble — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A multivitamin label warns against taking more than the recommended dose of vitamins A and D, but gives no such warning for vitamin C. Explain this in terms of solubility and storage in the body.

answer.model_answer_md: Vitamins A and D are fat-soluble: excess is stored in the liver and fatty tissue and can build up to harmful levels (hypervitaminosis). Vitamin C is water-soluble: excess is not stored but is excreted in urine, so overdose is far less likely.

questions.solution_md: Fat-soluble stored; water-soluble excreted.

questions.stem_md: Name the vitamin most likely to be deficient in each case, with the name of the condition where there is one: (a) a fisherman away at sea for months with only rice and dried fish develops bleeding gums; (b) a student with sore, cracked corners of the mouth who avoids milk and eggs; (c) a woman who has eaten a strict vegan diet for many years becomes anaemic.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Vitamin C — scurvy. (b) Vitamin B₂ — cheilosis. (c) Vitamin B₁₂ — pernicious anaemia (B₁₂ comes mainly from animal foods).

questions.solution_md: C; B₂; B₁₂.

questions.stem_md: A nutritionist plans meals for a hostel where most students are vegetarian and study indoors all day. Explain why the plan must (a) combine cereals with pulses to supply essential amino acids, (b) include fresh citrus fruit or amla every day, and (c) encourage some time outdoors in sunlight.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Essential amino acids cannot be made in the body; cereals are low in lysine and pulses supply it, so together they provide all essential amino acids. (b) Vitamin C is water-soluble and not stored, so it is needed daily; citrus and amla are rich sources (prevents scurvy). (c) Vitamin D is made in the skin in sunlight; indoor living risks deficiency (rickets, osteomalacia).

questions.solution_md: Essential amino acids; daily vitamin C; sunlight for vitamin D.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What are vitamins? Classify vitamins A, B₁, C, D, E and K as fat-soluble or water-soluble. [2]

(b) Name the disease or symptom caused by deficiency of (i) vitamin A, (ii) vitamin B₁, (iii) vitamin D and (iv) vitamin K. [2]

(c) Why are water-soluble vitamins needed in the diet regularly? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Organic compounds required in small amounts in the diet for normal growth and health. Fat-soluble: A, D, E, K. Water-soluble: B₁, C.

(b) (i) Night blindness / xerophthalmia. (ii) Beriberi. (iii) Rickets (children) / osteomalacia (adults). (iv) Increased blood-clotting time.

(c) They are not stored in the body; excess is excreted in urine.

questions.solution_md: Definition and classification; four deficiencies; not stored.

questions.stem_md: Which pair of bases found in DNA are both purines?
questions.solution_md: A and G are purines; C and T are pyrimidines — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which combination of sugar and base occurs in RNA but not in DNA?
questions.solution_md: RNA: ribose with A, G, C, U — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the Watson–Crick double helix, the two strands of a DNA molecule are:

options.text_md: parallel and identical in base sequence
antiparallel and complementary, held together by hydrogen bonds between bases
joined by peptide bonds between bases
held together by phosphate groups shared between strands

questions.solution_md: Option (b).

questions.stem_md: During protein synthesis, which nucleic acid brings each amino acid to the ribosome?
questions.solution_md: Option (d).

questions.stem_md: An RNA strand is built using a DNA strand with the base sequence G–C–A–T–T–A as a template. The base sequence of the RNA, read in the same direction, is:
questions.solution_md: G → C, C → G, A → U, T → A — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In any double-stranded DNA, the number of purine bases equals the number of pyrimidine bases.

**Reason (R):** Every base pair in DNA consists of one purine and one pyrimidine.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** RNA contains thymine as one of its bases.

**Reason (R):** The sugar in RNA is ribose.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false (RNA has uracil instead); R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? For a double-stranded DNA sample, the ratio of (adenine + guanine) to (cytosine + thymine) is equal to 1.
questions.solution_md: True: A = T and G = C, so A + G = T + C.

questions.stem_md: The double-helix model of DNA was proposed in 1953 by James Watson and Francis ___.
questions.solution_md: **Crick**.

questions.stem_md: A double-stranded DNA molecule of 2500 base pairs contains 700 adenine bases. How many cytosine bases does it contain?
Name the purine and pyrimidine bases present in DNA, and state the base-pairing rules, including the number of hydrogen bonds in each pair.

answer.model_answer_md: Purines: adenine, guanine. Pyrimidines: cytosine, thymine. Adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds; guanine pairs with cytosine through three hydrogen bonds.

questions.solution_md: Four bases classified; A–T (2), G–C (3).

questions.stem_md: Compare DNA and RNA with respect to (a) the pentose sugar and the pyrimidine bases, (b) the number of strands and overall structure and (c) their main biological roles.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) DNA: 2-deoxyribose; cytosine and thymine. RNA: ribose; cytosine and uracil. (b) DNA: two antiparallel strands in a double helix; RNA: usually a single strand. (c) DNA stores hereditary information and replicates; RNA (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA) carries out protein synthesis.

questions.solution_md: Sugar and bases; strands; roles.

questions.stem_md: Name the three main types of RNA in a cell and state the role of each in making a protein such as haemoglobin.

answer.model_answer_md: Messenger RNA (mRNA) carries the coded sequence copied from the haemoglobin gene in DNA to the ribosome. Transfer RNA (tRNA) brings the correct amino acids to the ribosome, each matched to the code. Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) forms part of the ribosome, where the amino acids are joined by peptide bonds.

questions.solution_md: mRNA, tRNA, rRNA with roles.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between a nucleoside and a nucleotide. [1]

(b) Classify the bases adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine and uracil as purines or pyrimidines, and state which occur in RNA. [2]

(c) Describe the double-helix structure of DNA. [1]

(d) A DNA molecule of 1200 base pairs contains 30% adenine. How many guanine bases does it contain? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Nucleoside = base + pentose sugar; nucleotide = base + sugar + phosphate.

(b) Purines: adenine, guanine. Pyrimidines: cytosine, thymine, uracil. RNA contains A, G, C and U.

(c) Two antiparallel polynucleotide strands wound round a common axis; sugar–phosphate backbones outside; bases inside, paired A–T (2 H-bonds) and G–C (3 H-bonds).

(d) Total bases $= 2 \times 1200 = 2400$; A = T = 30% each, so G = C = 20% each; G $= 0.20 \times 2400 = 480$.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; bases; helix; 480.
